query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the spray stand‐off distance to 60–80% of the current value will produce a significantly thicker FeCoNiCrAl high‐entropy alloy bond coat with a denser microstructure and minimal as‐sprayed oxidation, compared to the current coating deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high‐entropy alloy feedstock (15–45 μm, gas-atomized, near-spherical particles) deposited on a suitable substrate for thermal barrier coating (TBC) systems.
generation.intervention: Decrease the spray stand‐off distance by approximately 20–40% (e.g., from 100 mm to 60–80 mm) during thermal-spray deposition, while keeping all other parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Deposition under standard thermal-spray (e.g., HVOF or APS) conditions with inert gas shielding; the bond coat is intended for service under high-temperature conditions typical of TBC systems (up to ~1100 °C) in oxidizing environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Improved in-flight particle kinetics promotes efficient splat formation and inter-splat bonding, resulting in a denser and thicker coating.
generation.mechanism: A shorter stand-off distance reduces particle flight time, thereby preserving higher particle temperature and velocity. This minimizes oxidation and scattering, enhances splat flattening, and increases material capture on the substrate, leading to a thicker, integrity-preserving deposit.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention is expected to yield a bond coat with a thickness increased by approximately 50% or more relative to the baseline (e.g., from <45 μm to about 70 μm or higher), while maintaining low oxide content and robust adhesion.
generation.baseline: The existing bond coat, produced with a standard stand-off distance from 15–45 μm feedstock, exhibits an insufficient thickness along with acceptable, yet suboptimal, oxidation levels.
generation.boundary: The approach remains effective if the stand-off distance is not reduced so much that it causes excessive substrate heating or thermal stress, which could otherwise lead to coating defects or degraded adhesion.
generation.uncertainty: Potential uncertainties include the possibility that too short a distance might induce undesirable thermal effects (such as substrate overheating or altered phase composition) or lead to particle rebound, which would counteract the anticipated improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled series of thermal-spray depositions on FeCoNiCrAl substrates using different stand-off distances (e.g., control at 100 mm; experimental groups at 80 mm, 70 mm, and 60 mm) while keeping all other parameters constant. Post-deposition, assess coating thickness, oxidation level, and adhesion quality.
measurements: Coating thickness measurements via cross-sectional microscopy
Adhesion strength tests (e.g., peel or tensile adhesion tests)
Microstructural characterization (splat morphology, porosity) via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reduced stand-off distance does not yield a statistically significant increase in coating thickness (targeting ~50% improvement over baseline) or if it results in increased oxidation levels or compromised coating adhesion/integrity relative to the control, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). cited_evidence.kind: web:2.3. Atmospheric Plasma Spraying Coating of Samples
cited_evidence.text: Pre-heating of the processed HEA powder was carried out by placing it in the oven for 2 h at 25–150 °C, to remove any moisture present. The substrates were pre-heated with the flame of the spraying gun before the powder feed start. Plasma sprayed samples were manufactured by conventional Atmospheric Plasma Spraying system (Metco 9MC, Sulzer Metco Inc., Westbury, NY, USA) using a stand-off distance of 250 mm. Argon (Ar) gas was employed as the primary plasma operating gas and hydrogen (H2) was used as the secondary gas to escalate the whole plasma jet temperature. The feedstock ball milled powder was conveyed by a separate argon source and inoculated superficially into the spawned plasma jet at an angle of 90° concerning the anode axis. After that plasma torch assembly was mounted onto a robotic arm (YR-SK16-J00 Motoman, Yaskawa Electric Corp, Fukuoka, Japan) to navigate across the substrate holders for coating. papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.approach: HVOF deposition with variable spray distances to examine in‐flight oxidation and coating build‐up
papers.findings: Increasing the spray distance reduced the overall deposition thickness and increased coating porosity and oxide content. This suggests that shorter distances yield thicker deposits with less oxidation.
papers.mechanism: A reduced distance shortens the flight time, thereby preserving higher particle kinetic energy and minimizing in‐flight oxidation, which favorably enhances splat flattening and coating buildup.

papers.title: Microstructure and Corrosion Behavior of Atmospheric Plasma Sprayed NiCoCrAlFe High Entropy Alloy Coating.
papers.approach: Atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) with process parameter optimization including spray distance and substrate pre-heating
papers.findings: Optimized APS processing leads to coatings with improved adhesion, low oxide content, and superior mechanical integrity. Control over spraying parameters directly impacts both microstructure and oxidation.
papers.mechanism: Fine-tuning the thermal and kinetic conditions during spraying (e.g., by using a shorter stand-off distance) enhances particle in-flight conditions, reducing oxidation and promoting denser splat formation.

papers.title: Fabrication of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Coating on an AISI 304 Substrate via a CoFe2Ni Intermediate Layer.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA on AISI 304 stainless steel
papers.approach: Laser deposition utilizing a trochoidal toolpath designed to improve capture efficiency and mitigate powder scatter
papers.findings: A modified toolpath enlarged the melt pool and improved powder capture, resulting in coatings with enhanced thickness and uniformity.
papers.mechanism: The increased melt pool size and efficient capture reduce feedstock loss by minimizing scatter, indirectly supporting thicker, coherent coatings.

established: Coating thickness and porosity in thermal-spray processes are strongly influenced by spray distance; shorter distances can yield thicker, denser deposits.
In-flight particle temperature and kinetic energy control both oxidation levels and splat formation, which are critical for coating integrity.
Optimizing deposition parameters (e.g., spray distance, pre-heating, toolpath design) can mitigate excessive in-flight oxidation while enhancing coating buildup.

approaches_tried.approach: Varying spray (stand-off) distance in HVOF/APS deposition
approaches_tried.outcome: Longer distances lead to decreased thickness and increased oxidation/porosity; shorter distances improve deposition efficiency and minimize oxidation.

approaches_tried.approach: Modifying toolpath geometry to enhance melt pool size and capture efficiency
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved deposition yield and coating uniformity without compromising bonding, although this approach primarily addressed scatter rather than oxidation directly.

mechanisms: Reducing spray distance decreases in-flight time and minimizes oxidation while maintaining high particle velocity, thereby enhancing splat formation and coating thickness.
Enhanced capture efficiency (via toolpath modification) increases the proportion of feedstock that contributes to the coating, supporting thicker deposits.
disagreements: Some studies note that a certain degree of in-flight oxidation (forming oxide phases) can be beneficial for tribological performance, while bond coats for thermal barrier systems require minimal oxidation for proper adhesion and service life.

There is ongoing debate regarding the trade-off between maximizing deposition thickness and controlling oxidation versus potential thermal stresses or phase changes induced by too short a spray distance.
open_questions: Can simply reducing the spray distance be sufficient to overcome the coating thickness shortfall without introducing adverse thermal effects or deleterious microstructural changes?

How does an intervention focused solely on spray distance interact with other parameters (e.g., powder feed rate, particle size distribution) to affect both initial deposition quality and long-term bond coat performance under TBC service conditions?
opportunities: Investigate the use of a shorter stand-off distance during thermal spraying as a single intervention to boost coating thickness while preserving coating integrity and minimizing as-sprayed oxidation.

Evaluate process conditions (e.g., controlled substrate pre-heating combined with reduced spray distance) that might synergistically enhance deposition efficiency without compromising the oxidation resistance required for bond coat performance in thermal barrier coating systems.

directions.direction: Reduce the spray stand‐off distance during deposition
directions.assessment: This intervention directly targets the thickness shortfall by decreasing particle flight time, which preserves kinetic energy and limits in‐flight oxidation, yielding thicker, denser coatings. The evidence shows that shorter distances lead to better splat formation and reduced porosity (PMC10820071::web::010::3_2_oxidation_and_phase_transformations_, PMC8875499::web::007::2_3_atmospheric_plasma_spraying_coating_). It respects constraints by preserving minimal oxidation and integrity.

Enhancing the feed rate could supply more material, potentially addressing the thickness deficit. However, this may lead to increased particle scattering and oxidation if not balanced with other spray parameters, making it a less direct solution.

directions.direction: Optimize powder particle size distribution toward coarser particles
directions.assessment: A modified particle size could improve deposition efficiency and reduce oxidation, yet changing the feedstock properties might unintentionally affect splat formation and coating microstructure. It is less directly supported by the evidence compared with spray distance adjustments.

Pre-heating the substrate can improve splat adhesion and increase deposition efficiency. However, this intervention does not directly address the primary issue of feedstock thickness and may introduce thermal stresses that compromise coating service performance.

directions.direction: Employ supplemental inert shielding gas jets
directions.assessment: Enhancing the inert atmosphere around the spray path could further reduce oxidation losses. Nonetheless, while it may help preserve coating integrity, it does not directly overcome the thickness shortfall since it does not improve the deposition yield per se.

choice.direction: Reduce the spray stand‐off distance during deposition
choice.why: Reducing the stand‐off distance directly increases particle kinetic energy upon impact, minimizes in‐flight oxidation, and enhances splat flattening. This parameter adjustment is well supported by prior evidence and is a straightforward, single-variable intervention that should yield a thicker, denser bond coat without compromising the minimal oxidation requirement.
